newsitem.title: FRANCE: U.S. arrests Algerian Islamist leader -- radio.
newsitem.headline: U.S. arrests Algerian Islamist leader -- radio.

text.p: United States immigration officials have arrested a senior Algerian Moslem fundamentalist politician after rejecting his request for political asylum, France's private Europe 1 radio station reported on Wednesday.

It said official U.S. sources had confirmed that Anouar Haddam, self-styled leader of the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) parliamentarians in exile, had been in detention for five days pending expulsion.
France had pressed Washington to silence him since Moslem guerrillas carried out a wave of attacks on French nationals in Algeria and bombings in Paris, diplomatic sources said.

Europe 1 said Haddam, who signed a peace platform with secular Algerian opposition parties on behalf of the FIS in Rome in January 1995, had asked to be deported to Sweden, which has one of the most liberal asylum policies in Europe.

Haddam was elected to parliament in the first round of an Algerian general election in December 1991, but the army intervened to cancel the runoff in January 1992 and prevent an almost certain FIS victory.

The Islamic party was outlawed and its leaders either locked up or exiled. At least 50,000 people have been killed in the ensuing civil war between the military-dominated authorities and Moslem guerrillas.

Haddam and his family took refuge in the United States, where they have lived in Washington and Chicago for almost five years. State Department officials met him at a time when Washington was exploring a possible political solution in Algeria through dialogue with the Islamic opposition.

In July 1994, Haddam and another exiled FIS leader living in Belgium, Ahmed Zaoui, were expelled from the movement's official leadership in exile after endorsing the actions of radical Armed Islamic Group (GIA) guerrillas, who have targeted foreigners.

He later distanced himself from the GIA and represented the FIS at the Rome conference which established a platform for democracy and peace with the secular Socialist Forces Front (FSS) and the former ruling National Liberation Front (FLN).
The platform collapsed after military President Liamine Zeroual refused to deal with any of its signatories.
Algerian opposition sources said Haddam's influence in the movement was now marginal.
